title: Morning gratitude
hookLine: one thing you're glad of on waking
tomorrow: an emperor lists who will annoy him today. why on earth?

lines: DREAD BEFORE YOUR FEET HIT THE FLOOR.
A POET IN A RUINED CITY.
cards: Dread can wake up before you do: the inbox, the bill, yesterday's hard thing still waiting. The poet of Lamentations woke up to worse. Jerusalem had fallen, and the book is a long cry over the ruins.
Then, in the middle of it, he says: "It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness."

teach.b: Today's question: what should the first words of the day be? Jewish tradition answers with a short prayer said on waking, before getting out of bed, before even washing the hands: Modeh Ani, I give thanks.
In it you thank God, the living and lasting King, for returning your soul to you with compassion, and it ends with the poet's words from the ruins: great is your faithfulness. Here is the teaching.

teach.h: MODEH ANI: A SOUL GIVEN BACK.
teach.b: The Talmud calls sleep a small taste of death, so each waking is a soul given back, a gift, not a given.

teach.h: THANKS BEFORE THE DAY EARNS IT.
teach.b: Gratitude comes first, before you've done anything to earn the day. Not because the day is good yet. The poet said it standing in rubble.
The morning itself is the evidence. Now a neighbor.

teach.h: ISLAM'S WAKING WORDS: TO HIM IS THE RETURN.
teach.b: Islam keeps waking words too. Bukhari records that the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, would say on waking: praise be to God who gave us life after He had made us die, and to Him is the return.
And the Qur'an says God takes souls at death, and takes in sleep the souls that have not died, sending them back for a set term.
Shared: sleep as the soul held, waking as the soul returned, thanks as the first word.
An honest difference: Modeh Ani dwells on the soul restored and God's faithfulness; the Muslim words also look ahead, to the final return to God. Two prayers, each in its own house.

how: Jewish prayer books set Modeh Ani at waking, before getting out of bed, and Bukhari records the Prophet's waking words of praise; both thank God first thing for the return of the soul.

o: relief that a bad dream from the night is over
thanks given first thing, before the day has earned it
a list of goals you write down before breakfast

p: the Jewish prayer said on waking
the words Modeh Ani ends with
praise to God who gave us life

s: gratitude only counts once the day has gone well
the poet of Lamentations gave thanks in a ruined city: the mercies are new every morning.
Modeh Ani is said before getting out of bed
it's the first word of the day, before even washing the hands.
the Jewish and Muslim waking prayers are really one prayer
both thank God for waking; Modeh Ani dwells on the soul restored, the Muslim words also look to the final return.

games.q: your little brother asks why grandma thanks God the second she wakes up, 'before anything even happened.' what fits Modeh Ani?
o: waking is what happened: a soul given back, a mercy new that morning.
it's a habit, so she remembers to be polite for the rest of the day.
she thanks God in advance so that the rest of the day goes well.
games.why: in Modeh Ani, waking itself is the gift: God returns the soul with compassion. thanks comes first because the morning already happened.

practice: Name three things you're glad of right now, under your breath: something in this room, something in your body, someone in your life.
Keep each one small and specific, and stay with the third a little longer, the way the old waking prayers give thanks before anything else.

wordCard.voice: Morning gratitude: thanks as the first word of the day. In Jewish practice, Modeh Ani, for a soul given back.

orig.note: Hebrew: I give thanks, the opening words of the Jewish waking prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: glad to wake. The mercies are new before the day has done a thing. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.

sources.ref: Modeh Ani, the waking prayer (siddur; said before washing the hands)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 57b (sleep as one-sixtieth of death)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6312 (the Prophet's words on waking)
Qur'an 39:42 (God takes souls at death and in sleep, and sends back the rest for a term)
